dok_rationale: Part (c) adjudicates two displays, connects the baseline to distortion, contrasts apparent and actual magnitudes, and defends a second display choice for a stated purpose.
stem: Suppose 184 students chose a favorite lunch option. A newsletter printed \textbf{Graph A} with the headline ``\textbf{Pizza wins by a landslide.}'' A council member redrew the data as \textbf{Graph B} and said, ``It is basically a tie.''
first_take: Is pizza clearly the favorite? Name the graph that most influenced you.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Read the Pizza and Pasta counts. How many more students chose Pizza?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Convert all four counts to whole-number percents of 184. Describe how close the categories are in context.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: For ``Is pizza clearly the favorite?'' choose the more honest graph and name the design feature that settles it. Quantify Graph A's visible Pizza-to-Pasta heights, then compare 52 with 41 using percent increase. Finally, choose a zero-baseline bar graph or pie chart for comparing the four categories and defend that choice.

answers.a: Pizza has 52 students and Pasta 41, so Pizza has 11 more.
answers.b: Pizza $28\%$, Tacos $26\%$, Salad $24\%$, Pasta $22\%$ (rounded). The largest and smallest shares differ by about 6 percentage points, and none reaches $30\%$.
answers.c: Graph B: its zero baseline makes full bar height proportional to count. Graph A starts at 40, so visible heights are $12$ and $1$; Pizza looks 12 times as tall. In fact, $52/41=1.27$: only 11 students, about $27\%$ more (about a 6-point share lead). Pizza leads narrowly---neither a landslide nor a tie. Use the zero-baseline bar graph because aligned lengths reveal close differences; a pie chart emphasizes shares of a whole but its similar wedges are harder to compare.

expectedElements.description: Selects Graph B and connects its zero baseline to bar height representing count
Uses visible heights 12 and 1 to explain the apparent 12-times ratio
Contrasts that with 52 versus 41, 11 students, or about 27 percent
Defends bar or pie by what lengths versus angles or areas make easier to compare

scoringGuide.E: Chooses Graph B with the baseline mechanism, quantifies both apparent and actual differences, and defends a display for comparing close categories.
scoringGuide.P: Makes the graph decision but omits the mechanism or one numerical contrast, or gives only a generic display reason.
scoringGuide.I: Trusts Graph A's magnitude, treats 12 and 1 as counts, or gives no feature-based display choice.

commonMistakes: Calling Graph A's counts false instead of explaining its truncated baseline
Reading visible heights 12 and 1 as student counts
Saying 52 is $11\%$ more than 41 rather than dividing by 41
